newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Urals begin to attract foreign investment.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Urals begin to attract foreign investment.

text.p: Russia's industrial heart in the Ural Mountains dividing Europe and Asia is beginning to attract large-scale foreign investment for the first time.

"It's a bit like the airplane on the runway: the businessmen who are on board are going to do very, very well," said Ian Worthington, who heads the British Trade Chamber. "The question is when is the plane going to take off."

Companies such as PepsiCo Inc. and Coca-Cola Co. think the economy in the Urals capital Yekaterinburg (population 1.5 million) will take off soon and have recently unveiled plans to build major plants.

In February, Pepsi International Bottlers, a joint venture between PepsiCo and the U.S. investment company Leucadia National Corp., started building a soft drinks plant, an investment expected to cost $40 million by the factory's expected summer opening, said regional director Paul Sofianos.
"We're going to lose money for the first two or three years, but then we are going to make money," he said.
Britain's Inchcape Plc is also planning to invest more than $30 million to make Coca-Cola in a local plant and compete against long-time rival Pepsi.

Previously closed to foreigners because of its many defence plants, Yekaterinburg, Russia's fourth-largest city, has lately stepped up efforts to attract foreign investment, which started off slowly after the 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union.
Eduard Rossel, governor of Sverdlovsk province which includes Yekaterinburg, plans to travel to the United States, Canada and Britain in mid-March to drum up investment.
Such a trip might be nothing unusual for an American governor, but it is still new for Russian regional officials who until recently awaited economic marching orders from Moscow.

"My goal during these travels is to try to attract investment to our region, to show we are the most attractive place in Russia to invest," Rossel said in an interview. "For foreign investors, we have endless opportunities."
Among the opportunities are natural mineral resources, as well as heavy industry, much of it established in World War II as Soviet leaders sought a safe base far from enemy lines.
The region is also using high tech to lure investors. There is a home page on the Internet, and a computer CD-ROM singing its praises.

On paper, the reasons for investment are compelling. In addition to its industrial base, Yekaterinburg, home town of President Boris Yeltsin, strongly supports economic reform and has a well-educated population.

"Sometimes I think this will be the next emerging market, the Urals. Here they have only a few players so it's an open market," said Daniel Billman, regional director of the U.S.-Russia Investment Fund, which makes loans to small businesses. "I think opportunity is there as well as risk."
"If you like bungee jumping, roller-coaster diving, this is the place to be," added one foreign official.

Foreign investors put $80 million into the region around Yekaterinburg last year, a figure which is about three to five times higher if direct stock purchases are factored in, said Vladimir Lomovtsev, head of the Sverdlovsk region foreign investment department.

Among the more than 50 firms with foreign representative offices are Germany's Dresdner Bank AG, Britain's Flemings bank, and Caterpillar Inc., which has a joint venture with the massive Uralmash factory.
Yet foreign investors who do try to set up shop encounter an often-bewildering maze of local and federal rules.
Even finding out what incentives the government is willing to offer must typically be worked out case-by-case. "It is very difficult to get a written brief of incentives," Worthington said.

Some local officials also remain wary of foreigners, who were kept out of much of the region until the fall of Communism. "There is a layer which hates foreign investment because they fear foreign competition," said Lomovtsev. "They fear everything will be bought by foreigners."
With such challenges, most foreign firms have limited their involvement so far to trade.

For example, since setting up three years ago Wm. Wrigley Jr. Co. has built a chewing gum market share of 76 percent locally, with sales of 100,000 cases a month worth almost $1 million, said Olga Salyayeva, customer service manager.

Japanese company Mitsui and Co. does tens of millions of dollars of business in the region annually exporting minerals from Russia and selling machinery, said acting regional manager Igor Fishelev. Mitsui is working on a deal to sell the Uralmash factory more than $50 million in equipment, he said.

But bureaucracy has thwarted others. U.S. officials complain that levying by the Sverdlovsk region of a 50 percent tax on chicken imports is a worrying sign of capricious legislation that could hurt other investors.
